title: EDUCATION | 5.24.26 The Death of the University Degree
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Carl Hendrick argues that the university degree has fundamentally changed as a diagnostic instrument since ChatGPT's arrival in 2023, and that this change has not been adequately reckoned with. Princeton's May 2026 faculty vote to end its 133-year honor code -- requiring proctoring for all in-person exams because the 'social contract' underpinning unsupervised assessment has collapsed -- is the emblematic moment. Author Katherine Rundell called the phenomenon a 'vast counterfeiting of knowledge' at Hay Festival: universities are raising a white flag by reclassifying AI use as legitimate scholarship if footnoted, making it now possible to write an essay about a book without having read it. Citing Michael Spence's signaling theory, Hendrick argues the degree's 'separating equilibrium' has broken down: AI substitution has decoupled finishing coursework from actually learning the material, so transcripts no longer reliably differentiate students who did the work from those who did not. Labor market consequences are emerging: Russell Group AI misuse cases tripled in one year; UK youth unemployment is at an 11-year high of 16.2%; and employers are beginning to discount the credential accordingly.
points: * Princeton ended its 133-year honor code in May 2026 -- the unsupervised exam tradition survived two world wars, Watergate, and the rise of search engines but could not survive ChatGPT, signaling a fundamental collapse of the social contract in higher education. * The degree's 'separating equilibrium' has broken down: on Michael Spence's signaling account, the credential's value depended on completion being more costly for low-ability students -- AI substitution has severed that coupling between finishing work and learning. * Katherine Rundell named the dynamic at Hay Festival: a 'vast counterfeiting of knowledge' -- universities raising a white flag by reclassifying AI-assisted work as legitimate scholarship if footnoted, making it possible to write essays about books without reading them. * Russell Group universities formally disciplined over 2,000 students for AI misuse in a single academic year, triple the prior year's figure of roughly 700 -- and these are only the cases formally adjudicated. * UK youth unemployment stands at a 16.2% eleven-year high, with 946,000 sixteen-to-twenty-four-year-olds not in education, employment, or training -- many holding degrees that employers are beginning to discount as AI-produced credentials flood the labor market.
quotes: Does anyone seriously believe that a degree completed in 2026 is the same diagnostic instrument as one completed in 2016, or indeed, any time before ChatGPT showed up in 2023?
It is now possible to write an essay about a book without having read the book. -- Katherine Rundell, Hay Festival 2026
She called what is happening a 'vast counterfeiting of knowledge,' and accused universities of raising a 'white flag' by reclassifying AI use, provided it is footnoted, as legitimate scholarship.

A 2016 graduate accumulated knowledge under a regime in which finishing the work and learning the material were tightly coupled. A 2026 graduate has accumulated, in part, a track record of finished work whose coupling with learning is now an open question.
The credential no longer reliably differentiates between students who did the work and students who did not, on precisely the dimensions where AI substitution is easiest.
